summary: Harald Kirschner introduces a progression from "YOLO vibe coding" to "spec-driven vibes," addressing how vibe coding can scale in enterprise environments. The framework has three stages. First, YOLO vibe coding—coined by Andrej Karpathy—focuses on outcomes over code, using natural language iteration and auto-accepting changes. It suits rapid prototyping, personal projects, and learning AI capabilities, but is not meant for production. Second, structured vibe coding introduces templates with consistent tech stacks, instructions guiding Copilot toward team conventions, and custom tools via MCP for reliable context retrieval. This bridges creative prototyping to engineering handoff. Third, spec-driven vibes target large codebases with scale and reliability, following a repeat cycle: start with a spec, make a plan, then implement the plan. A live demo builds a React water hydration tracking app using VS Code Insiders agent mode, showcasing built-in voice dictation (local model), a create-new-workspace tool, chat auto-approve for reduced friction, auto-save for live updates, and undo/revert for course correction. The AI reads terminal errors and self-corrects dependency installation issues. Model differences are noted: Claude 4 excels at UI, 4.1 produces wireframe-like results, and 2.5 Pro has varied design aesthetics. VS Code chat modes are introduced—defined in a GitHub folder, they allow specifying tools and system prompts per mode, enabling custom agents like a test-driven development agent that writes tests first and only proceeds to code after user review. Prompts enable reusable team tasks such as generating standardized landing pages for design teams. Instructions files outline what specific codebase parts do and can be made dynamic for different codebase sections. VS Code's integration with problems and tasks allows AI to auto-fix code using linter and task runner output. MCP provides additional context retrieval, though it was not demoed due to time. Best practices include committing workable code frequently via the spark icon and pausing the agent to inspect, preventing regressions. Spec-driven vibes bring these practices to enterprise scale with specs, plans, task-specific tools, and more MCPs.

sections.title: Introduction and Three Stages of Vibe Coding
sections.summary: Kirschner introduces vibe coding as coined by Andrej Karpathy and defines three progressive stages: YOLO vibes (fast, creative, no code review, not for production), structured vibes (templates, guardrails, consistent tech stacks, engineering handoff-ready), and spec-driven vibes (large codebase scale with reliability). He positions the talk as a journey from chaotic YOLO coding to professional zen vibes.

sections.title: YOLO Vibe Coding Demo
sections.summary: Live demo building a React water hydration tracking app using VS Code Insiders agent mode. Features shown include built-in voice dictation (local model), create-new-workspace tool, chat auto-approve, auto-save for live updates, and undo/revert. The AI self-corrects terminal errors for dependency installation. Model design differences noted: Claude 4 good for UI, 4.1 wireframey, 2.5 Pro varied aesthetics. YOLO coding is positioned as a skill-building exercise for AI intuition.

sections.title: Structured Vibe Coding and Templates
sections.summary: Structured vibe coding introduces templates with consistent tech stacks and instructions guiding Copilot toward team conventions. Custom tools via MCP provide reliable context retrieval. A front-end vibes template on GitHub is shown as an example. This approach benefits non-mainstream frameworks by adding explicit instructions, makes vibe coding accessible to non-technical users, and produces engineering-ready output aligned with internal standards like Fluent UI.

sections.title: Chat Modes and Custom Agents
sections.summary: VS Code chat modes are introduced as customizable agents defined in a GitHub folder, where teams specify available tools and system prompts per mode. Custom agents like a test-driven development agent can be created with specific instructions. This enables teams to codify workflows and guide AI behavior toward specific methodologies, bridging creative vibe coding with structured enterprise practices.

sections.title: Prompts, Instructions, and Spec-Driven Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Kirschner elaborates on prompts as reusable team tasks (e.g., generating standardized landing pages), instructions files that outline what specific codebase parts do, and workspace instructions made dynamic for different codebase sections. He references VS Code's problems and tasks integration, where properly configured linters and task runners let AI auto-fix code. MCP is mentioned but not demoed due to time. Best practices include committing workable code frequently via the spark icon and pausing the agent to inspect. Spec-driven vibes are summarized as a repeat cycle: start with a spec, make a plan, implement the plan—bringing these practices to enterprise scale with prompts, MCPs, and task-specific tools.
